sections.title_en: 1. The Mitzva of Releasing the Fruit
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to release and abandon the fruit of the field in the seventh year, as it is said (Shemot 23:10-11): "And six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce. But the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beast of the field shall eat. In like manner you shall deal with your vineyard and with your olive grove."

Since the mitzva is to release the fruit, it is ownerless for everyone: for the poor and for the rich, for Jews and for non-Jews, for people and for animals (below 9). And what is said, "that the poor of your people may eat," is because this is the main novelty: that in the shemita year the poor too can enjoy the fruit like the owners of the fields. And so it was in practice, that most of the fruit of Shevi'it was eaten by the poor. For apart from the owners of the fields, who lived near their fields and would gather from them for the needs of their household, it did not pay for the rich to go through all the fields in order to gather for themselves; but for the poor this trouble was worthwhile (Mekhilta de-Rashbi Shemot 23:11).

The mitzva of shemita applies to the fruit only and not to the land and the trees. Therefore those who come to eat of the fruit may not cut the branches of the tree, and likewise they may not stay there without the permission of the owner of the field, because they were permitted to enter the field only in order to pick the fruit.

The main mitzva is to make the fruit ownerless, and there is no mitzva to eat it; rather it is permitted to leave it on the trees as food for the animals and the birds. And there is one who holds that there is a mitzva in eating the fruit of shemita; and although the view of the great majority of the poskim is not like his, those who are meticulous try to eat fruit of Shevi'it.1

The fruit that one is commanded to make ownerless is the fruit that grew in Shevi'it. And since we have already learned (in the previous chapter) that it is a mitzva to rest in Shevi'it from the work of the field and the trees, the yield of the fields in Shevi'it would shrink to about twenty percent of the usual yield. For usually most of the yield of the fields comes from annual crops of grain, legumes and vegetables, and since one does not sow or plant in Shevi'it, about seventy percent of the yield is consequently not to be found. And indeed by Torah law aftergrowths (sefiḥim) that grew by themselves are permitted to be eaten, but the Sages decreed that they not be eaten, because of transgressors who would sow in the shemita and claim that these were aftergrowths that grew by themselves (below 4). The only field crops that have the law of Shevi'it are vegetables that began to grow on the eve of Shevi'it and are picked in Shevi'it, which must be released (below 6). It follows, then, that the main yield of Shevi'it was from the fruit of trees; but it too would shrink in the shemita, since it is forbidden to do kinds of work that help the growth of the tree and the fruit (above 2:3). If so, when we speak of the fruit of Shevi'it, we are speaking of about twenty percent of the total yield that would grow in the other years.

notes_en.en: The Ramban wrote, in the positive commandments the Rambam omitted, 3, that the Rambam omitted the mitzva to eat it and not to trade with it; and this mitzva is repeated in Shemot 23:11: "that the poor of your people may eat," and it does not say only to leave the fruit, as is said regarding the gifts for the poor. And some learned from this (Mahari"t Algazi, Tzitz Ha-Kodesh and others) that in his view there is a mitzva to eat the fruit of shemita. And most of the Aḥaronim wrote, on the basis of the Rishonim who did not mention this mitzva, that there is no mitzva to eat fruit of Shevi'it. And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 24:6; Torat Ha-Aretz 8:25-28. And some wrote that the Ramban too agrees with this (Ḥazon Ish 14:10; Seridei Esh 2:116). And Maran Rav Kook wrote that it appears from the words of the Ramban that there is a mitzva (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 6:1, 2), and he recommended being meticulous in this (Da'at Kohen 240), but he wrote that by the letter of the law there is no mitzva in this (Kuntres Aḥaron 21).

sections.body_en:
When the fruit on the trees becomes fit to eat, the owners of the fields must open the gates of their fields, so that anyone who wishes to pick from them can enter. And anyone who leaves his field locked at a time when the fruit on the trees is fit to eat cancels a positive mitzva. And even if he picks the fruit in order to distribute it to the poor, since he locked his field he has cancelled the mitzva, because the mitzva is to release the field (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael Mishpatim, parasha 20; Rambam 4:24). And if he did not lock his field but reaped or picked his whole field in the manner of owners, even if he did so in order to distribute it to the poor, he has transgressed the prohibition of reaping or harvesting grapes (below 3).

By the basic law one would have to breach the fence, to show by this that the fruit is ownerless for all. But for the sake of the good order of the world the Sages permitted not breaching it, so as not to damage the fence, and so as not to open too wide an opening for animals or hooligans who would enter and damage the trees (Mekhilta there). However, if the fence was breached by itself, it is forbidden to fence it in Shevi'it. And if the fence was breached on the side of the public domain, and there is a concern that many people will enter the field and damage it, it is permitted to fence that side (Rambam 2:14).

The owner of the field need not announce that the fruit that grew in his field is ownerless, for by the commandment of the Torah it becomes ownerless, and any person may enter the fields of Israel and pick fruit from them. However, if the owner of the field insisted on forbidding people to enter his field, although he transgresses the commandment of the Torah and steals the fruit, nevertheless, since the field itself is his, they may not trespass on his boundary; and because of his seizure of his fruit they become obligated in terumot and ma'asrot out of doubt (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 6:15; Introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 11).

According to Beit Shammai the one who gathers the fruit may not thank the owner of the field for it, and all the more so he may not give him a gift for it, since the fruit of Shevi'it is ownerless, and one who thanks the owner of the field impairs the force of the ownerlessness. But the halakha follows Beit Hillel, that a person may choose how to act: if he wishes not to thank, let him not thank; and if he wishes, he may thank the owner of the field for giving him permission to enter his field to gather of the fruit (Mishna Shevi'it 4:2; Rambam 6:15). And so it is fitting to act from the outset: to ask permission to enter the field and to give thanks for the fruit.2

When the owner of the field has a reasonable concern that if he opens his field to all, hooligans will come and damage his trees, he may lock his field and write on a prominent sign that the fruit is ownerless, and anyone who wants to pick from it can receive the key at such-and-such a place, or that the field will be open at such-and-such hours (based on the Ḥazon Ish, Mishpetei Eretz 10:4).

notes_en.en: Plainly the field becomes ownerless by itself, for that is the mitzva, and this is a 'removal by the King' (Bava Metzia 39a). And so it is understood from the words of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim (Ra'avad and Rash of Sens, Mabit 1:11; Mahari"t 1:43; Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 62; Maharsham 3:101; and many others). However, the Minḥat Ḥinukh 84 wrote that there is a dispute about this: according to the Mabit the fruit is ownerless by itself, and according to the Beit Yosef it is not ownerless by itself. But in truth the Beit Yosef did not decide so. And it is not possible that according to the Beit Yosef one would need to renounce ownership explicitly, when the Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not write this. And Maran Rav Kook explained his view, that one need not renounce ownership explicitly, but that if he fenced his field and showed in practice that he does not renounce it, although he transgressed the commandment of the Torah, the fruit that grew in his field is not ownerless (Introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 11, Mishpat Kohen 82). And so wrote the Ma'amar Mordechai p. 178. (And see Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:24, 4.) Therefore, if the field is not open, one should ask permission, in order to make sure that the owner of the field has made his fruit ownerless. And one should also join the view of the Ra'avad and Rash of Sens on Eduyot 5:1, who wrote that the Sages forbade entering fields without the owners' permission, lest people become accustomed to entering and stealing fruit in the other years. In summary, when the owner of the field forbids entry to the field, although he transgresses a prohibition, entry is forbidden. And not only this, but it is right to take into account the view of Rash of Sens and the Ra'avad, who hold that one must ask permission of the owner of the field to enter. And one may say that according to their view, after the owner of the field gives permission, according to Beit Shammai it is forbidden to thank him, and according to Beit Hillel it is permitted to thank him. And it seems that since he is already asking permission, it is good that he thank him in order to increase peace. Some are meticulous to say aloud that the fruit is ownerless, and so wrote the Da'at Kohen 240.

sections.title_en: 3. The Prohibition of Reaping and Harvesting Grapes
sections.body_en:
In addition to the positive mitzva to release the fruit of Shevi'it (above 1-2), the Torah added two more negative prohibitions. One, not to reap the grain of the field as people are accustomed to reap in all the years; and the second, not to harvest the grapes of the vineyard or pick the fruit of the other trees in the way people do in all the years. As it is said (Vayikra 25:5): "That which grows of itself of your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of your undressed vine you shall not gather; it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land." Rather, all shall be equal in the fruit of Shevi'it, and the owners of the fields shall take with the other people, each according to his need, as it is said (ibid. 6): "And the Sabbath produce of the land shall be food for you: for you, and for your servant and for your maid, and for your hired servant and for the settler by your side who sojourn with you."

The amount that each person may bring from the field is the amount of food that people are accustomed to bring home from the field or from the shop in the other years. Of fruit that keeps for a short time, they were accustomed to bring a quantity sufficient for a few days; and of fruit that keeps longer, they would bring for a few weeks; and if it kept a long time they would bring a quantity sufficient for a number of months. And this is what the Sages said, that of olives one may take the amount from which one makes five jars of oil, and of grapes the amount from which one makes fifteen jars of wine (Rambam 4:24). And those who sin and gather more fruit than they need are called 'gatherers of Shevi'it', and they are disqualified from giving testimony, because their deeds show that the lust for money drives them out of their senses (Sanhedrin 26a; Yad Ramah there).

From the time of removal (bi'ur), that is, the time when all the fruit of that species is gone from the fields, one who has in his house more than the food for three meals is commanded to remove it from his house, that is, to distribute it anew, so that each person will take of it the amount of three meals and no more. And if he is unable to distribute it, he should take it out of his house and make it ownerless. And the other laws of removal will be explained below (4:10-11).

Fruit that people are accustomed to process after picking, such as grapes that are pressed for wine, olives pressed for oil, and figs dried in a drying-yard, must be processed in a changed way: to make them in smaller vessels or with another change, so that there will be a sign that they are fruit of Shevi'it, and people will not come to trade in them and will remember to make them ownerless at the time of removal (Mishna 8:6; Rambam 4:23).

Some hold that even when one is careful not to pick more than the amount of household use, one must change the manner of gathering, so that it will not be with the same vessels with which one gathers in all the years. But in practice there is no obligation to change, because gathering limited to the amount needed for the household is considered a sufficient change.3

notes_en.en:
The Sages said (Sifra Behar 1:3): "'You shall not gather' – in the manner of those who harvest grapes." According to the Rash and the Rosh, the meaning is that he should not gather his fruit in the manner of an owner who does not let strangers enter his field; but if he made it ownerless, he may, like anyone else, harvest the whole vineyard as in all the years. But according to the great majority of the Rishonim, even in a field that was made ownerless it is forbidden to harvest in the manner of those who harvest, among them: Tosafot, Rabbeinu Tam, the Ra'avad, the Razah. And so wrote the Rambam 4:1: "If he reaped in the manner of reapers he is flogged, for example if he reaped the whole field; rather he reaps a little at a time, threshes and eats." And there, 24: "And he may bring into his house a little, in the way one brings from ownerless property." However, there is still a difference between the Torah prohibition of reaping or harvesting the whole field and the permission to bring a little at a time. And in my humble opinion, with reaping or harvesting a quantity of a field, even if it is small, he is flogged. And the Ma'adanei Eretz (3:3) wrote that it is the amount of making a pile. But if he took less than that and more than he needs for his household, although he did not transgress the prohibition of reaping and harvesting, he cancelled the positive mitzva of releasing, whose essence is that the fruit be ownerless for everyone to eat, for by taking more he prevented them from eating it. And it seems that he also transgressed the rabbinic prohibition of reaping and harvesting by gathering more than his household needs.
According to the Gra it is forbidden to reap or pick with a tool, only by hand, and this is what the Torah forbade to reap and harvest (Shenot Eliyahu 8:6). And some say that it is indeed permitted to pick with a tool, but not with a tool one is accustomed to pick with in all the years (Tosafot Rosh Ha-Shana 9a; Ra'av 8:6), so that people will not come to pick more than is permitted. And some say that one need not change the manner of gathering, but the main change is that he gathers for his household needs and not as in the other years (Rambam 4:24; Ḥinukh 328; Sha'arei Tzedek 16:1). And we have followed this way in explaining the sugya, that the main prohibition is to pick a large quantity, and all the changes the Sages mentioned relate to this alone.
And some inclined to be stringent and forbid picking more than the amount of food for three meals (Sefer Ha-Shemita 3, 12, in the name of Rav Ḥaim Berlin). And some wrote that it is permitted to bring fruit in the quantity one is accustomed to bring for household use for a few days (Mishpetei Eretz 11:3). And their reasoning is very difficult, for the mitzva of removal is to distribute food for three meals to many people (Mishna 9:8; below 4:10), so even those who kept shemita properly had in the house much more than food for three meals and the use of a few days. And it is further difficult for them from the fact that they permitted gathering the amount of five jars of oil and fifteen jars of wine, as the Rambam wrote, 4:24, on the basis of Mishna 5:7. Rather, one is forced to say that since the fruit is ownerless for all, a person may take of it in the way people are accustomed to take in all the years for household use, according to the number of people. And consequently the matter depends on the kind of fruit: of those that rot quickly one brings for a few days, and of those that keep a long time one brings for a number of months, as they explained regarding oil and wine. And similarly wrote the Ḥazon Ish 26:2; and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Ma'adanei Eretz 7:2-3. And so wrote the Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 12, 11. And in my humble opinion a person may add and pick also for his relative or neighbour, in order to save him the trouble of going to the field, on condition that it is clear that everything he brings from the field is meant for household use. And when many sinned and took for themselves more than their household use, they made a fence for the matter and set up guards who did not let people bring home more than the food for three meals (Tosefta Shevi'it 8:1).

sections.body_en:
By Torah law all aftergrowths (sefiḥim), that is, the kinds of plants that grew by themselves in Shevi'it, are permitted to be eaten, and all the laws of fruit of Shevi'it apply to them. But when the Sages saw that transgressors were sowing kinds of vegetables, grain and legumes in secret, and afterwards claiming that these crops grew by themselves, they decreed that all the kinds of annual plants that came up in a Jew's field are forbidden. But plants that renew themselves every year from their roots, since there is no need to sow them in Shevi'it in order to eat their fruit, have no prohibition of aftergrowths. Therefore there is no prohibition of aftergrowths with mint and bananas.

The prohibition of aftergrowths applies to field crops that people are accustomed to sow or plant in their fields; but wild plants that came up by themselves are permitted, for since their price is cheap and people are not accustomed to grow them, there is no concern that transgressors will sow them in the shemita (Rambam 4:3). And likewise it is permitted to eat aftergrowths that grew in places where people are not accustomed to sow, such as in a place where they harm the other crops, or in an ownerless field, since there is no concern that transgressors will sow there (ibid. 4; Ma'amar Mordechai 11:29). And in any case, even where there is no decree on aftergrowths, the fruit that grew in Shevi'it is holy with the holiness of Shevi'it.4
It is also worth noting that the decree on aftergrowths applies within the borders settled by those who came up from Babylon, and not within the borders of those who came up from Egypt, nor across the Jordan (Rambam 4:26-28). And likewise the decree on aftergrowths applies to what grows in land belonging to a Jew and not to what grows in land belonging to a non-Jew (ibid. 29).

With grain and legumes, the determining time for tithes and Shevi'it is the 'reaching of a third'. If they reached a third of their growth before the Rosh Ha-Shana of the seventh year, their law is like fruit of the sixth year. And if they reached a third after Rosh Ha-Shana, their law is like fruit of Shevi'it, and the prohibition of aftergrowths applies to them (ibid. 9; Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:3).

Regarding vegetables there is a dispute. According to the Rambam, any vegetable that remained attached to the ground after the Rosh Ha-Shana of the seventh year is forbidden under the law of aftergrowths, because the determining time for it is the picking. And according to several Rishonim, anything that began to sprout in the sixth year, even though it was picked in Shevi'it and the holiness of Shevi'it applies to it and it must be made ownerless, the prohibition of aftergrowths does not apply to it (Rash). And so it is accepted to rule. Vegetables that began to grow in Shevi'it and finished their growth in the eighth year are forbidden until the time when vegetables like them could grow from sowing or planting at the end of Shevi'it, or once Ḥanukka arrives (see Rambam 4:6-7).5

notes_en.en:
According to Rabbi Akiva the prohibition of aftergrowths is from the Torah, but according to the Sages the prohibition is rabbinic (Sifra Behar 3:5, and see Pesaḥim 51b). And so ruled the Rambam 4:1-2. Perennial vegetables that renew themselves every year from the root have no decree of aftergrowths (Rambam 4:3); therefore there is no prohibition of aftergrowths with mint, banana and papaya. Regarding the banana there is a further reason for there being no prohibition: it gives fruit a year and a half after its planting, and the prohibition of aftergrowths applies only to something that gives fruit within its year (Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 3, 122:7).
Some say that one should uproot aftergrowths that grew by themselves, so that people will not say that he intends to eat them; and some say that it is forbidden to uproot them, because they have the holiness of Shevi'it and it is forbidden to destroy them (see Harḥavot to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:18, 4). And the right course is not to touch them, but what he sowed in transgression should be uprooted (Ma'amar Mordechai 11:10).

We find in the Mishna a discussion of vegetables that have the holiness of Shevi'it (Shevi'it 7:3; 8:4; 9:1). The Rash and the Rosh learned from this that vegetables that began to grow in the sixth year and were picked in Shevi'it have no prohibition of aftergrowths but do have the holiness of Shevi'it. And so is the view of Tosafot and the Ritva. And it seems that this is also the view of the Ramban; and the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 22:3 explained that according to the Ramban, only if they ripened in the sixth year do they have no prohibition of aftergrowths. By contrast, the view of the Rambam (4:9-10; 4:12) is that whatever was picked in Shevi'it has the prohibition of aftergrowths. And so ruled the Semag, Rash Sirillo and the Mabit. But the view of most of the Aḥaronim is like the view of the Rash (Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan, Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:3; Sefer Ha-Shemita, Ḥazon Ish). In addition to the fact that in a dispute over a rabbinic matter the halakha follows the lenient view, and the view of most of the poskim is also to be lenient, it is also reasonable: for the whole prohibition is because of transgressors, and there is no prohibition at all against planting in the sixth year. Therefore any field that was sown and began to sprout before the shemita has no prohibition of aftergrowths.

sections.title_en: 5. The Time of Growth of the Fruit of Shevi'it
sections.body_en:
The determining time for the fruit of trees is the ḥanata (budding of the fruit), which is the time at which it can be eaten in a pressing situation, and the time at which it becomes obligated in tithes; in the language of the Sages it is called reaching a third of its ripening. It follows that fruit that budded in Shevi'it has the holiness of Shevi'it even though it continued to grow in the eighth year; and if it budded in the sixth year, even though it continued to grow in Shevi'it, it does not have the holiness of Shevi'it, and the owner of the orchard may pick it as in all the years. However, from the time the seventh year begins it is forbidden to carry out kinds of work that improve the tree and the growth of the fruit (some hold that the ḥanata is the beginning of the growth of the fruit; and the law of the etrog and citrus fruits will be explained in the note).6

Regarding field crops, we have already learned that most of them were forbidden because of the decree on aftergrowths (above 4); but there are some that were not forbidden, namely: plants that renew themselves from their roots every year, such as the banana; and likewise what grew by itself in ownerless fields or in places where a person does not want them to grow; and likewise what sprouted before Shevi'it. However, regarding the stage that determines the holiness of Shevi'it, there is a difference between grain and legumes on the one hand and vegetables on the other.

The determining time for grain and legumes is the 'reaching of a third', when they are fit to be eaten in a pressing situation, that is, they have ripened to the extent of a third. If they were sown in the sixth year and reached a third before Shevi'it, they have no holiness. And if they reached a third in Shevi'it, they have holiness (Rambam 4:9).

And the determining time for vegetables is the time of their picking. Therefore, if they sprouted before the shemita and were picked in Shevi'it, they have the holiness of Shevi'it. And the same is the law of annual seasoning plants.7

notes_en.en:
According to the Rambam and the Semag, the determining time for Shevi'it is the season of tithes. And it is explained in Mishna Ma'asrot 1:1 that the beginning of the time of tithes is when the fruit begins to be fit to eat in a pressing situation, and the same is the law regarding Shevi'it. And it is the time at which their seeds can grow (Rambam, Shemita and Yovel 4:9; Ma'aser Sheni 2:3-5). And the Mahari Korkos, Rash Sirillo, the Penei Yehoshua and others explained that ḥanata and the season of tithes are, according to the Rambam, one time. On the other hand, according to Tosafot (Rosh Ha-Shana 12b, s.v. 'Ha-tevu'a'), the time of ḥanata is before the time of tithes. And many explained that it is the first appearance of the small fruit (Meiri, Kaftor Va-Feraḥ). For the halakha the ruling follows the Rambam (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 23:7; Sefer Ha-Shemita and others; and Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:9 and Mishpat Kohen 3 inclined to this). And several Rishonim wrote that the season of tithes is like the time of reaching a third, which is mentioned regarding grain and legumes (Rosh Ha-Shana 13b) as the time of their obligation in tithes. But they were in doubt about the definition of a third: some say a third of the volume, some say a third of the weight, and some say a third of the ripening (see Harḥavot to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:9, 2). And one is forced to say that the main definition is a third of the ripening, that is, a third of the development of the taste, when it is already fit to be eaten in a pressing situation, like the eating of ben Drosai in the laws of cooking on Shabbat. And those who explain a third of the volume and the weight are apparently speaking of certain fruits that even when they have reached a third of their weight are fit to be eaten in a pressing situation; but most fruit at this stage is not fit to be eaten even in a pressing situation.
And some hold that since the new year for trees is the fifteenth of Shevat, only fruit that budded between the fifteenth of Shevat of the seventh year and the fifteenth of Shevat of the eighth year is holy with the holiness of Shevi'it (Rabbeinu Ḥananel, the Shelah). But the view of most of the poskim is that the fifteenth of Shevat is the new year as regards the years of tithes and orla for the tree, but as regards Shevi'it the first of Tishrei is the new year, as they said in the Mishna (Rosh Ha-Shana 2a): "On the first of Tishrei is the new year for years and for the shemita years." And so wrote the Rambam 4:9; the Radbaz, Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan, Sha'arei Tzedek, Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Sefer Ha-Shemita. And so it emerges from Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:9. And so wrote the Ma'amar Mordechai 12:9; and Mishpetei Eretz 15:1.
The etrog and citrus fruits: according to most of the Tanna'im and Amora'im, the law of Shevi'it for the etrog is determined by the ḥanata, and according to our Rabbis at Usha by the picking (Rosh Ha-Shana 14-15, Sukka 39b; 40a). And among the Rishonim, some hold that one follows the ḥanata (Ra'avad, Ritva, and so it is implied from several other Rishonim). And some say that one follows the picking (Rambam 4:12; Semag, Shulḥan Arukh 331:126). And some explained that the Rambam intended to be stringent with the etrog and follow also the picking (Ma'aseh Roke'aḥ). In practice one is stringent according to both views, and so wrote the Ma'amar Mordechai 12:13. And regarding the other citrus fruits, some hold that with them too one must be stringent as with the etrog (Ma'amar Mordechai 12:14). But according to many, citrus fruits are like the other fruits of the tree (Maran Rav Kook, Rav Herzog). And so it is practised (Ketif Shevi'it 6:7; Mishpetei Eretz 15:7-8).

The difference between vegetables and legumes is that with legumes the seed is the food, whereas with vegetables the food is the leaves, like lettuce and cabbage, or a fruit that has seeds inside but whose main part is not a seed, like squash and tomatoes. And there are exceptions, namely rice, millet and sesame: although they are included among grain and legumes, since the time they reach a third is not uniform, it was established that with them one follows the completion of the fruit (Rambam 4:11).
The Rambam wrote (4:12) that with vegetables one follows the picking, and it is implied even if they did not continue to grow in Shevi'it. And this is implied even more in the laws of Ma'aser Sheni (1:4). And in the Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 331:126, he wrote like the Rambam (and it seems that the Rambam follows his own view, 4:11, that one must fix one time for everything picked together; for if the time of a third or the time of the completion of growth were counted, things picked together might have different times). However, Tosafot (Rosh Ha-Shana 13b, s.v. 'Aḥar') hold that one follows the completion of the growth of the fruit, and if it was completed in the sixth year, even though it was picked in Shevi'it, its law is like fruit of the sixth year (and it seems that their view is that one follows the drawing of nourishment from the earth: with vegetables according to the end of drawing from the earth, and with the fruit of trees, already once they budded they finished drawing from the earth, and the tree has enough strength to grow the fruit until it ripens).
And according to all views, if they did not water the vegetables for thirty days before Rosh Ha-Shana, even though they picked them after Rosh Ha-Shana, their law is like fruit of the sixth year, since all their drawing of nourishment was in the sixth year only (Rambam 4:17). And so wrote in practice Ketif Shevi'it 6:11; Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 10, 5.
The determining time for the holiness of Shevi'it in annual seasoning or fragrant plants is the picking. And the same is the law with soft branches of perennial bushes (Ketif Shevi'it 6:8, 5). But with woody branches of perennial bushes it is the beginning of the formation of the branch (Ma'amar Mordechai 13:60-61), and it is hard to know when that is (see Ketif Shevi'it 6:14, 2). And if it is a flower, there is room to say that the determining time is the time the bud appears (Be-Tzet Ha-Shana, Ketif Shevi'it 6:14, 1).

sections.title_en: 6. The Fruit to Which the Mitzvot of Shevi'it Apply
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of releasing applies to all the produce of the land that is meant as food for people and animals, including grasses meant for eating, such as lettuce as human food and hay as animal food. And likewise to plants and leaves meant for seasoning, which are among the plants eaten by people. And every person may pick of this produce of the land for the needs of his household. It is called 'fruit of Shevi'it', and it is considered holy, that is, one must be careful about its purpose for eating, as it is said (Vayikra 25:6): "And the Sabbath produce of the land shall be food for you." The Sages expounded: 'for food' and not for trade (Avoda Zara 62a; below 5:6-9); 'for food' and not for waste, and any use that is not according to its usual purpose is considered waste (Pesaḥim 52b; below 4:1).

The laws of Shevi'it also apply to fruit and grasses meant for anointing the body or for dyeing clothes, since the benefit from them is similar to the benefit of eating. What characterises the benefit of eating is that it comes together with the consumption of the food, for the food is consumed as a person chews, swallows and digests it. And likewise with anointing the body with oil: at the time of the benefit the oil is consumed. And likewise with dyeing clothes with fruit: when the fruit is cooked with the garment, the fruit is consumed and the colour passes into the garment (Rashi).

But to wood and grasses meant for firing an oven for heating the house or for cooking, the holiness of Shevi'it does not apply, since first the wood is burned and only afterwards does one benefit from the heat that spreads through the house and from the dish that is cooked (Sukka 40a). And likewise wood from which furniture is made, or flax and cotton from which threads and clothes are made, has no holiness, since they are not like food, for they are not consumed.

The holiness of Shevi'it does not apply to kinds of plants meant for medicines, since they are meant for the sick only, unlike foods, which are meant for everyone.

The laws of Shevi'it do not apply to ornamental flowers that have no fragrance; but the Sages were in doubt regarding plants meant for fragrance. In practice, when their main purpose is fragrance it is right to be stringent, and when their main purpose is ornament one may be lenient.

A lulav and hadas for the mitzva have no holiness of Shevi'it.

It is important to note that the whole discussion in this section concerns the holiness of the fruit; but the prohibition of kinds of work meant to make things grow applies to all kinds of plants, including species that have no holiness.8

notes_en.en:
In the Yerushalmi 7:1 they were in doubt whether spices have the holiness of Shevi'it, and the Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 9:16 was lenient, because Shevi'it is rabbinic. But the accepted ruling is to treat them as holy (Sefer Ha-Shemita 7:4, 5; Ketif Shevi'it 5:4, 1; Mishpetei Eretz 14:1). However, regarding flowers meant for ornament which incidentally have a fragrance, one should be lenient (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach). And some are stringent even with flowers that have no fragrance, for their benefit as ornament and their consumption come together (Ma'amar Mordechai 13:64). And since shemita is rabbinic and most of the poskim are lenient, this is the halakha (Ketif Shevi'it 5:3, 2). And one should add that the benefit of sight is very far from the benefit of eating, for the benefit does not come from the consumption of the fruit. And it is different even from the benefit of fragrance: for although the benefit does not cause its consumption, nevertheless the fragrance enters the body like food, and the soul enjoys it, whereas sight does not enter the body at all. Regarding the determining time for the holiness of Shevi'it in fragrant plants, see the end of note 7.
In the past the lulav was used as a broom, and when people benefited from it, it was consumed; therefore the holiness of Shevi'it applied to it (Sukka 40a). And today, when people are not accustomed to sweep with it, it has no holiness (Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 1, 51:23). And likewise it is clear that there is no holiness in the hadasim of the mitzva, even though they have a fragrance, since they are meant for the mitzva (Ketif Shevi'it 5:3, 3-4).
In the past plants such as borit were used for laundering, and they had holiness. And today they are not used for laundering and they have no holiness, as explained in the next halakha, that if in practice the fruit is not used it has no holiness. Regarding mushrooms, the view of many is that they have no holiness, since they do not grow from the earth, for they have no roots (Rav Tzvi Pesaḥ Frank, Mishpetei Eretz 14:12; Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 9:3). And the view of Maran Rav Kook and Rav Yisraeli is that they have holiness (Ketif Shevi'it 5:4, 3). And today, when it is customary to grow them inside greenhouses in separation and detachment from the ground, according to all views they have no holiness of Shevi'it. And see above 2, note 13, regarding water-grown crops. Cotton seeds have the holiness of Shevi'it, for they are fit as animal food and for producing oil as human food (see Ketif Shevi'it 5:4, 2). In crops that have no holiness there is also no decree of aftergrowths (Minḥat Shlomo 51:11).

sections.body_en:
It is permitted to cut a branch of a fruit tree for a great need, for example if it interferes with walking on the path, or when its wood is worth more than the fruit it gives. And likewise in Shevi'it it is permitted to do so before fruit begins to grow on the branch, or after the fruit has ripened and become fit to eat; but from the time the branch begins to put out fruit until the fruit becomes fit to eat, it is forbidden to cut the branch or the fruit on it, because by cutting it he destroys the fruit that has begun to grow (Shevi'it 4:7-10; Rambam 5:15-18).

And even when the owner of the field is not accustomed to eat of the fruit that grows on this tree in his field, he may not cut from it a branch on which fruit has begun to grow; for the fruit of Shevi'it is meant for eating and it is forbidden to destroy it, and if he cuts the branch he will destroy the fruit and rob the public, who could have benefited from it (Mishna Shevi'it 4:10; Rash, Rosh and Rambam there).

Fruit fit to be eaten in a pressing situation also has the holiness of Shevi'it, and even if it is fit to be eaten by animals in a pressing situation (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 7:13, 3). However, if in practice people are not accustomed to use it for eating, it has no holiness, even though it would be possible to feed it to animals. Therefore there is no holiness of Shevi'it on grass and weeds that grow in the garden, since people are not accustomed to give them as animal food. And the same law applies to plants that were used in the past for making dye or for laundering, whose use in our time has ceased entirely: the holiness of Shevi'it does not apply to them, and it is permitted to destroy them or to use them for fuel. And the same law applies to peels and seeds: if people are not accustomed to eat them, they have no holiness of Shevi'it (below 4:2).9

notes_en.en:
Some wanted to establish a dispute over whether one follows what is 'fit', that is, if the fruit is fit to be eaten in a pressing situation, even though people are not accustomed to eat it at all, it has holiness; or whether one follows what it 'stands for', that if in practice people are not accustomed to eat it or to feed it to animals, it has no holiness (see Ketif Shevi'it 5, note 4). But in truth we have found no view holding that one follows what is 'fit'; rather everything is according to what is practised in fact. And so it is explained in the Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 14:10; Ma'asrot 1:30. And likewise in Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 1, 51:23, regarding the lulav. And likewise in Responsa Az Nidberu 4:66, regarding grass. And regarding orange peels there is no dispute, but everything depends on the reality: Maran Rav Kook (Mishpat Kohen 84) spoke of a reality in which people ate them, and consequently they had holiness; and the Ḥazon Ish spoke of a reality in which people did not eat them, and consequently they have no holiness.
It seems to me in my humble opinion that what they explained in Mishna Shevi'it 4:7-10 and Rambam 5:15-18, that it is permitted to pick fruit that has reached a third, being fit to eat in a pressing situation, applies at a time when people were indeed accustomed to eat it in a pressing situation. But today, when even in a pressing situation people are not accustomed to eat fruit that has reached a third of its ripening, it is forbidden to pick a branch or fruit until the fruit in practice reaches the state in which people today are accustomed to eat it in a pressing situation. However, if the picker wants to eat it already from when it reaches a third, he may pick it in order to eat it.

sections.title_en: 8. Fruit That Was Guarded, and Fruit Grown with Forbidden Work
sections.body_en:
The poskim disagree about the law of fruit that was guarded. Some say that although the owner of the field cancelled the positive mitzva of releasing the fruit, the fruit itself is permitted to be eaten, since by law the fruit belongs to everyone, and it is not possible for an individual to forbid it (Rash, Ramban, Rashba). And some say that only fruit that was made ownerless is permitted to be eaten, but fruit that was guarded in Shevi'it is forbidden to be eaten by Torah law (Rabbeinu Tam, Ra'avad). In practice, the view of most of the poskim is to be lenient; but it is forbidden to buy this fruit from the one who guarded it, so as not to assist transgressors.10

If a person transgressed and worked his field in the shemita, for example by pruning the trees and thereby increasing the quantity of the fruit and improving its quality, some say that the fruit is forbidden; for we have learned that a field that was ploughed in Shevi'it may not be sown at the end of Shevi'it, all the more so fruit that grew in violation of a prohibition is forbidden. And some say that although he transgressed a prohibition, the fruit itself is permitted to be eaten, because everything that grows in the shemita belongs to everyone, and it is not possible to forbid it. And so is the view of most of the poskim, and so is the halakha.11

notes_en.en:
According to most of the poskim, Rishonim and Aḥaronim, fruit that was guarded is permitted to be eaten. And so is the view of the Rambam as the Mahari Korkos explained (4:24; 8:10). And although we find that the Sages penalised one who ploughed his field in Shevi'it, that he may not sow it in the eighth year, so that he will not benefit from the work of Shevi'it, that is because in the eighth year the field and the fruit belong to the owner of the field, and it is possible to penalise him for what he did in Shevi'it. But the fruit of Shevi'it is ownerless, and there is no room to forbid it. (See the notes to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:1, 2.)
However, there is another law in this: we learned in the baraita in Sukka 39b that the permission to buy from an am ha-aretz who is suspected regarding Shevi'it the amount of food for three meals applies only when it is known that he brought it from ownerless produce; but if he brought it from guarded produce, it is forbidden to buy from him even a small amount. And Rashi explained that this is because we are concerned that he will not be careful about the prohibition of trade with the money he receives. And the Ritva added: so as not to strengthen the hands of transgressors. And in my humble opinion, when it concerns the owner of the field, it is agreed according to all views that one who buys from him transgresses the prohibition of strengthening the hands of transgressors.

The Rambam wrote, 4:1, that a field that was improved in Shevi'it in order to improve its fruit, its fruit is permitted to be eaten. And he further wrote (there, 15) that if he transgressed and sowed vegetables in Shevi'it, if they were picked in the eighth year they are permitted, for with vegetables one follows the picking (but in Shevi'it they are forbidden because of the decree on aftergrowths). By contrast, according to the Ra'avad the vegetables are forbidden, for we have learned that one who plants a tree in the shemita must uproot it, and likewise it is forbidden to keep what was sown, and the fruit is forbidden to be eaten. Similarly the Ramban wrote, Yevamot 122a, regarding fruit that was guarded, that it is permitted; but if he worked the trees and improved them, the fruit is forbidden. And the Rashba and the Ritva brought his words. However, the view of most of the poskim is to be lenient like the view of the Rambam; and so is the view of Tosafot Ha-Rosh (Shevi'it 4:2), the Mahari Korkos, the Radbaz, Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 22, Beit Yisrael 21, and others. And so wrote the Ma'amar Mordechai 10:13. (See the notes to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:15, 2.)

sections.title_en: 9. Non-Jews and the Fruit of Shevi'it
sections.body_en:
Although the fruit is completely ownerless and non-Jews may pick from it, from the outset, when there are Jews who want to eat all the fruit, it is right to prevent non-Jews from picking it, lest they not be careful about its holiness and waste it, and lest they trade in it, and lest they pick more of it than their household needs. In addition, we find in the Torah that the main aim of making the fruit ownerless is that "the poor of your people" may eat of it (Shemot 23:11), and it is not fitting that people who are not partners in the mitzva, who if they had a field would not need to make it ownerless, should come to benefit from the fruit of the shemita. And in the towns near the border they were more careful, and would set up guards to prevent non-Jews from coming and plundering the fruit of Shevi'it (Tosefta 4:4; Rambam 4:30).

After the fruit has been picked and is in a Jew's hands, the Sages established a prohibition against giving of it to a non-Jew. For since it is in a Jew's hands, he has an obligation to preserve the holiness of its purpose, which is to be eaten by Israel, and giving it to a non-Jew is considered waste. But a Jew may feed fruit of Shevi'it to a non-Jewish guest or hired worker who eats at his table, for his eating is considered part of the Jew's eating (Tosefta 5:21; Rambam 5:13; Mahari Korkos).

As is known, there is a possibility of 'selling' fruit of Shevi'it within the framework of an 'otzar beit din', in which case the payment is for the work and not for the fruit. And if a non-Jew came to a shop that 'sells' fruit of Shevi'it of an 'otzar beit din' and asked to buy from it, if the shop appears to be meant for everyone, since if he does not sell to the non-Jew he will be offended, it is permitted to sell to him in order to prevent enmity. But if it is a private sale, since there is no reason for him to be offended, one should not sell to him.12

Although the fruit of Shevi'it is ownerless, it is permitted to prevent animals from entering the field and eating of fruit attached to the tree which people intend to eat (see Tosafot Rosh Ha-Shana 9a, s.v. 'Ve-katzir'). Nevertheless there is no obligation to do so, since this fruit is ownerless. But after he has picked it, it has become designated as human food, and if an animal went to eat of it, he is obliged to prevent it (Rambam 5:5).13

notes_en.en:
The mitzva of releasing requires making the fruit ownerless for all, including non-Jews (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 6:1). However, in Tosefta Shevi'it 4:7 they said: "The towns of the Land of Israel that are near the border, one sets a guard over them so that non-Jews will not spread out and plunder the fruit of Shevi'it," and so wrote the Rambam 4:30. And the Radbaz there inclined to say that although one does not prevent poor non-Jews from receiving gifts for the poor together with the poor of Israel, because of the ways of peace (Gittin 59b), it is right to prevent them from gathering fruit of Shevi'it because it has holiness. However, it seems that all this is from the outset, but by the letter of the law they may pick, for by Torah law the fruit is ownerless for all. But if there is a concern that non-Jews will come and plunder a lot of fruit, the Sages ruled that one is obliged to prevent them from doing so, because the fruit is meant for the household use of Israel and not so that non-Jews will come and plunder everything for themselves. It further seems that if in any case there are no Jews who want to eat the fruit, it is clear that it is preferable that decent non-Jews pick it and eat it, on condition that they do not trade in it.
After a Jew has already picked the fruit, the Sages established that it is forbidden to give of it to a non-Jew, and of course it is forbidden to give of it to an animal (Tosefta 5:20-21). And the Mahari Korkos and the Mahari"t (1:43) explained that since it is meant to be eaten by Israel, giving it for another purpose is considered, for a Jew, as waste. Thus far. And the prohibition is rabbinic. And although the Sages said (Torat Kohanim Behar 1:7): "'For you for food' – and not for others," according to the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan and Maran Rav Kook the meaning is that the laws of shemita apply to fruit that grew in land of Israel and not of non-Jews (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 20). And some explain that this is an asmakhta (Ḥazon Ish 13:26).
But when the non-Jew is a guest or hired worker of a Jew, according to the great majority of the poskim it is permitted to give him fruit of Shevi'it to eat (Ḥasdei David there; Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 24, se'if katan 58; Shabbat Ha-Aretz 5:13). And according to the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 24:4 there is no prohibition at all against giving non-Jews fruit of Shevi'it, and what they said in the Tosefta not to give them fruit of Shevi'it refers to repaying a debt.
When fruit of Shevi'it is 'sold' in a shop on behalf of an 'otzar beit din' (ordinary fruit of Shevi'it may not be sold in a shop), and a non-Jew came and asked to buy: some say that one should not sell to him (Rav Elyashiv), and some say that one sells to him because of enmity, which is a weightier consideration than 'the ways of peace' (Rav Nissim Karelitz; brought in Perot Shevi'it p. 297). And see further below 8:5, regarding the export of fruit of Shevi'it abroad, in a way that it is likely non-Jews will buy of it.

In the Gemara, Menaḥot 84a, we learned that it is permitted in the shemita to guard barley so that animals will not eat it, in order to offer the omer from it. And Tosafot Rosh Ha-Shana 9a, s.v. 'Ve-katzir', explained that to people they would say that the barley is designated for the omer and by this they would keep away; but animals had to be kept away by hand in order to keep it for the omer. And from here we learned that although in Shevi'it everything is ownerless even for animals, nevertheless it is permitted to keep animals away from fruit that people are about to take. And see the Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 14:4, who permits locking a field against animals; and according to Rav Tykocinski in Sefer Ha-Shemita 2, 4, only when there is a concern that they will damage the tree is it permitted to lock it against them.
